intro.baseline: This questionnaire measures how you currently recognize, evaluate, and construct arguments in professional settings. Respond based on what you actually do now, not what you think you should do. There are no right or wrong answers.
intro.debrief: You completed this questionnaire at the start of the module. Answer again based on how you behave now. Then reflect on the module.

subscales.name: Fallacy Awareness
subscales.help: Recognizing why reasoning goes wrong and when you are most vulnerable.

items.text: I can explain why even experienced leaders are prone to errors in reasoning.
I recognize when a decision is being driven by fast, intuitive judgment rather than deliberate analysis.
I can name common logical fallacies when I encounter them in workplace communication.
I am aware of the situations in which I am most vulnerable to flawed reasoning.
I notice when a persuasive message relies on how it makes people feel rather than on its logic.

subscales.name: Relevance Evaluation
subscales.help: Judging whether the reasons offered actually bear on the claim.

items.text: I can distinguish an argument that attacks a person from one that addresses the person's position.
I recognize appeals to authority, popularity, or emotion that substitute for evidence.
If a respected leader supports a proposal, I am usually confident the reasoning behind it is sound.
I check whether the evidence offered for a claim is actually related to the claim.
I can identify when a discussion has been redirected to an issue that is not the one at hand.

subscales.name: Presumption Detection
subscales.help: Surfacing the hidden assumptions built into how a case is framed.

items.text: I question the assumptions built into how a problem is framed before evaluating the options.
I recognize when a choice is presented as either/or when other options exist.
I notice when a predicted chain of consequences is asserted without evidence for each link.
I can tell when an argument's conclusion is already assumed in its premises.
When I am confident in a position, I rarely look for evidence that could prove me wrong.

subscales.name: Argument Construction
subscales.help: Building reasoning that can withstand challenge.

items.text: I can state the conclusion and the supporting premises of my own arguments clearly.
I test each premise of my arguments to see whether it is a fact, an inference, or an assumption.
I anticipate the strongest objections to my recommendations before I present them.
I can evaluate the logical structure of an argument separately from whether I agree with its content.
I treat disagreement as an opportunity to improve my reasoning rather than as a contest to win.
This module improved my ability to recognize flawed reasoning in professional settings.
The observation scenarios helped me see how fallacies operate in real organizational discussions.
The simulation gave me realistic practice at evaluating and constructing arguments.
I feel more confident challenging weak reasoning in my leadership practice.
I would recommend this kind of practice to other leadership students.

open_ended.prompt: Describe the most important insight about logical fallacies you gained from this module.
Which moment in the observation or simulation had the greatest impact on you, and why?
How will you apply what you learned about sound reasoning in your leadership practice going forward?
